claim: Retrotransposons comprise around 40% of mammalian genomes.
source: Retrotransposons are mobile genetic elements that comprise around 40% of mammalian genomes (Beck et al., 2011; Hancks and Kazazian, 2016; Richardson et al., 2014a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Beck et al., 2011; Hancks and Kazazian, 2016; Richardson et al., 2014a

claim: New retrotransposition events are estimated to occur in around 1 in every 20 human births.
source: New retrotransposition events are estimated to occur in around 1 in every 20 human births, and represent around 1% of genetic disease-causing mutations in humans (Kazazian, 1999; Hancks and Kazazian, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kazazian, 1999; Hancks and Kazazian, 2016

claim: Retrotransposition events represent around 1% of genetic disease-causing mutations in humans.
source: New retrotransposition events are estimated to occur in around 1 in every 20 human births, and represent around 1% of genetic disease-causing mutations in humans (Kazazian, 1999; Hancks and Kazazian, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kazazian, 1999; Hancks and Kazazian, 2016

claim: In humans, all new retrotransposition events are catalysed by LINE-1 (L1) elements.
source: In humans, all new retrotransposition events are catalysed by LINE-1 (L1) elements.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: Active L1s encode two proteins strictly required for retrotransposition: ORF1p and ORF2p.
source: Active L1s encode two proteins strictly required for retrotransposition (Moran et al., 1996): ORF1p is an RNA binding protein with nucleic acid chaperone activity (Martin and Bushman, 2001; Hohjoh and Singer, 1997), and ORF2p is a multidomain protein with reverse transcriptase and endonuclease activities (Feng et al., 1996; Mathias et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moran et al., 1996; Martin and Bushman, 2001; Hohjoh and Singer, 1997; Feng et al., 1996; Mathias et al., 1991

claim: ORF1p is an RNA binding protein with nucleic acid chaperone activity.
source: ORF1p is an RNA binding protein with nucleic acid chaperone activity (Martin and Bushman, 2001; Hohjoh and Singer, 1997)
evidence: Supported by citations to Martin and Bushman, 2001; Hohjoh and Singer, 1997

claim: ORF2p is a multidomain protein with reverse transcriptase and endonuclease activities.
source: ORF2p is a multidomain protein with reverse transcriptase and endonuclease activities (Feng et al., 1996; Mathias et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Feng et al., 1996; Mathias et al., 1991

claim: P16 Tex19.1−/− testes have elevated levels of mL1-ORF1p.
source: Western blotting showed that P16 Tex19.1−/− testes have elevated levels of mL1-ORF1p (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1A

claim: L1 RNA levels do not change in P16 Tex19.1−/− testes compared to controls.
source: even though L1 RNA levels do not change (Figure 1B), as previously shown (Ollinger et al., 2008; Reichmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1B and citations to Ollinger et al., 2008; Reichmann et al., 2012

claim: Tex19.1 negatively regulates mL1-ORF1p post-transcriptionally in male germ cells.
source: These data suggest that Tex19.1 negatively regulates mL1-ORF1p post-transcriptionally in male germ cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mL1-ORF1p levels increase without changes in L1 RNA levels in Tex19.1−/− testes

claim: mL1-ORF1p is expressed in meiotic spermatocytes in control mice.
source: Immunostaining of P16 testes showed that, consistent with previous reports, mL1-ORF1p is expressed in meiotic spermatocytes in control mice (Figure 1C) (Soper et al., 2008; Branciforte and Martin, 1994).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1C and citations to Soper et al., 2008; Branciforte and Martin, 1994

claim: mL1-ORF1p immunostaining is elevated approximately two fold in spermatocytes in Tex19.1−/− mice.
source: However, mL1-ORF1p immunostaining is elevated approximately two fold in the same cell type in Tex19.1−/− mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantified immunostaining data in Figure 1C

claim: TEX19.1-YFP immunoprecipitates from mouse ESCs contain multiple components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system.
source: mass spectrometry of TEX19.1-YFP immunoprecipitates (IPs) from stably expressing mouse ESCs revealed co-IP of multiple components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (Figure 2A, Figure 2B, Supplementary file 1, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2A, 2B and supplementary files

claim: TEX19.1-YFP IPs contain UBR2 as a co-immunoprecipitating band of approximately stoichiometric abundance to TEX19.1-YFP.
source: TEX19.1-YFP IPs contained a strong co-immunoprecipitating band of approximately stoichiometric abundance to TEX19.1-YFP which was identified as UBR2, a RING domain E3 ubiquitin ligase and known interacting partner for TEX19.1 (Yang et al., 2010) (Figure 2A, Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry and Western blot data in Figure 2A, 2B and supplementary figures, and citation to Yang et al., 2010

claim: All detectable endogenous TEX19.1 in ESCs co-fractionates with UBR2 in size exclusion chromatography.
source: Indeed, all detectable endogenous TEX19.1 in ESCs co-fractionates with UBR2 in size exclusion chromatography (Figure 2C)
evidence: Supported by size exclusion chromatography data in Figure 2C

claim: TEX19.1 exists in a stable heteromeric complex with UBR2 in ESCs.
source: consistent with TEX19.1 existing in a stable heteromeric complex with UBR2 in these cells.
evidence: Inferred from co-fractionation and stoichiometric abundance data

claim: Ubr2 is required for TEX19.1 protein stability in mouse testes.
source: Importantly, Ubr2 has previously been shown to be required for TEX19.1 protein stability in mouse testes (Yang et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2010

claim: TEX19.1-YFP co-IPs with UBE2A/B, an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme and cognate partner of UBR2.
source: TEX19.1-YFP also co-IPs with additional components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system including UBE2A/B, an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme and cognate partner of UBR2 (Kwon et al., 2003; Xie and Varshavsky, 1999)
evidence: Supported by co-IP data in Figure 2B and citations to Kwon et al., 2003; Xie and Varshavsky, 1999

claim: TEX19.1-YFP co-IPs with HUWE1, a HECT-domain E3 ubiquitin ligase.
source: and a HECT-domain E3 ubiquitin ligase, HUWE1 (Chen et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2005) (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data in Figure 2B and citations to Chen et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2005

claim: The post-transcriptional increase in mL1-ORF1p abundance in Tex19.1−/− testes reflects a role for TEX19.1 in regulating degradation of mL1-ORF1p.
source: The physical associations between TEX19.1 and multiple components of the ubiquitin-proteasome system strongly suggest that the post-transcriptional increase in mL1-ORF1p abundance in Tex19.1−/− testes might reflect a role for TEX19.1 in regulating degradation of mL1-ORF1p.
evidence: Inferred from the physical associations between TEX19.1 and ubiquitin-proteasome system components

claim: TEX19.1-YFP and mL1-ORF1p-T7 physically interact.
source: Both IPs revealed weak reciprocal interactions between TEX19.1-YFP and T7 epitope-tagged mL1-ORF1p (mL1-ORF1p-T7) (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C

claim: The physical interaction between TEX19 and L1-ORF1p is conserved in humans.
source: Although human TEX19 is significantly truncated relative to its mouse ortholog, the physical interaction between TEX19 and L1-ORF1p is conserved in humans (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D

claim: Co-expression of mL1-ORF1p-T7 with TEX19.1-YFP results in co-localization of both proteins in cytoplasmic aggregates in 25 of 51 cells examined.
source: As expected, confocal microscopy showed that TEX19.1-YFP localizes to the nucleus when expressed in U2OS cells, however co-expression with mL1-ORF1p-T7 resulted in some co-localization of both these proteins in cytoplasmic aggregates in 25 of 51 cells examined.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data described in the text and shown in Figure 2F

claim: TEX19.1-YFP interacts with a mutant allele of mL1-ORF1p which has severely impaired binding to RNA.
source: TEX19.1-YFP is able to interact with a mutant allele of mL1-ORF1p which has severely impaired binding to RNA and impaired L1 mobilization (Kulpa and Moran, 2005; Martin et al., 2005) (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F)
evidence: Supported by co-IP data in Figure 2E and citations to Kulpa and Moran, 2005; Martin et al., 2005

claim: The interaction between TEX19.1-YFP and mL1-ORF1p is RNA-independent and could potentially be direct.
source: suggesting that the interaction between TEX19.1-YFP and mL1-ORF1p is RNA-independent and could potentially be direct.
evidence: Inferred from the interaction with RNA-binding mutant of mL1-ORF1p

claim: Co-expression of double-tagged human MBP-TEX19-GB1-His6 with Strep-tagged human L1-ORF1p in bacteria results in a strong interaction between these proteins.
source: Notably, co-expression of double-tagged human MBP-TEX19-GB1-His6 with Strep-tagged human L1-ORF1p (Strep-hL1-ORF1p) in bacteria resulted in a strong interaction between these proteins, and isolation of a stable TEX19-hL1-ORF1p complex (Figure 3A, Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by bacterial pull-down assay data in Figure 3A and 3B

claim: The interaction between bacterially expressed TEX19 and hL1-ORF1p is resistant to micrococcal nuclease treatment.
source: This interaction required the proteins to be co-expressed (Figure 3A) and was resistant to micrococcal nuclease treatment (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by micrococcal nuclease treatment data in Figure 3B

claim: TEX19 recognizes the conserved and previously crystallized part of the hL1-ORF1p trimer.
source: Furthermore, TEX19 was found to recognize the conserved and previously crystallized part of the hL1-ORF1p trimer (Khazina et al., 2011; Boissinot and Sookdeo, 2016) and the N-terminal half of hL1-ORF1p that lacks the RNA-binding domains (Figure 3C, Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data with L1-ORF1p fragments in Figure 3E and citations to Khazina et al., 2011; Boissinot and Sookdeo, 2016

claim: The first 68 amino acids of TEX19, which contain the conserved MCP region and a putative Zn2+-binding motif, are necessary and sufficient for the interaction with L1-ORF1p.
source: In addition, the first 68 amino acids of TEX19, which contain the conserved MCP region and a putative Zn2+-binding motif (Bianchetti et al., 2015) were found to be necessary and sufficient for the interaction (Figure 3D, Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by pull-down assay data with TEX19 fragments in Figure 3F and citation to Bianchetti et al., 2015

claim: TEX19 directly interacts with L1-ORF1p in a conserved manner.
source: Taken together, the co-IPs, the co-localization and the isolation of a TEX19:L1-ORF1p complex from bacterially expressed proteins suggest that TEX19 directly interacts with L1-ORF1p in a conserved manner
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of experimental evidence including co-IPs, co-localization, and bacterial pull-downs

claim: TEX19 represents the first example of a host protein that directly binds to the retrotransposon-encoded protein L1-ORF1p from mammals.
source: and, to our knowledge, represents the first example of a host protein that directly binds to the retrotransposon-encoded protein L1-ORF1p from mammals.
evidence: Stated as a novel finding based on the authors' knowledge of the field

claim: There is basal ubiquitylation of hL1-ORF1p in HEK293T cells.
source: HEK293T cells do not endogenously express detectable levels of TEX19 (Reichmann et al., 2017) and cell-based ubiquitylation assays show that there is basal ubiquitylation of hL1-ORF1p in these cells, detectable as a ladder of hL1-ORF1p species in his6-myc-Ub pull-downs (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by cell-based ubiquitylation assay data in Figure 4A and citation to Reichmann et al., 2017

claim: hL1-ORF1p abundance is negatively regulated by the proteasome in the absence of TEX19 expression.
source: Furthermore, treating these cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 showed that hL1-ORF1p abundance is negatively regulated by the proteasome in the absence of TEX19 expression (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by proteasome inhibitor treatment data in Figure 4B

claim: Co-expression of TEX19 increases polyubiquitylation of hL1-ORF1p.
source: Interestingly, co-expression of TEX19 during the cell-based ubiquitylation assay increases polyubiquitylation of hL1-ORF1p (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by cell-based ubiquitylation assay data in Figure 4C

claim: TEX19 expression increases the proportion of hL1-ORF1p-T7 that has at least four ubiquitin monomers.
source: TEX19 expression increases the proportion of hL1-ORF1p-T7 that has at least four ubiquitin monomers, the minimum length of polyubiquitin chain required to target proteins to the proteasome (Thrower et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by quantified ubiquitylation data and citation to Thrower et al., 2000

claim: Expression of TEX19 reduces the abundance of T7-tagged hL1-ORF1p protein without any change in the abundance of its encoding RNA.
source: Nevertheless, expression of TEX19 in these cells is sufficient to reduce the abundance of the T7-tagged hL1-ORF1p protein without any change in the abundance of its encoding RNA (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4D

claim: Expression of either mouse or human TEX19 orthologs reduces both mouse and human L1-ORF1p levels in hamster XR-1 cells.
source: The ability of TEX19 to regulate L1-ORF1p abundance is not restricted to HEK293T cells, and expression of either mouse or human TEX19 orthologs reduces both mouse and human L1-ORF1p levels in hamster XR-1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and 1C

claim: TEX19 orthologs function to post-translationally regulate L1-ORF1p abundance.
source: Taken together, these gain-of-function data for TEX19 mirror the loss-of-function data obtained from Tex19.1−/− testes, confirm that the increased mL1-ORF1p levels in Tex19.1−/− testes are not a consequence of altered progression of Tex19.1−/− spermatocytes through meiosis (Crichton et al., 2017b; Ollinger et al., 2008), and strongly suggest that Tex19.1 orthologs function to post-translationally regulate L1-ORF1p abundance.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of gain-of-function and loss-of-function data, with citations to Crichton et al., 2017b; Ollinger et al., 2008

claim: TEX19 orthologs regulate L1-ORF1p abundance by molecular recognition of L1-ORF1p and stimulation of its polyubiquitylation and proteasome-dependent degradation.
source: The ubiquitylation and interaction data together suggests that, TEX19 orthologs regulate L1-ORF1p abundance by molecular recognition of L1-ORF1p and stimulation of its polyubiquitylation and proteasome-dependent degradation.
evidence: Inferred from combined ubiquitylation and interaction data

claim: Expression of Tex19.1 reduces the ability of both a codon-optimized Tf type and a natural Gf type mouse L1 to mobilize in HEK293T cells.
source: Notably, expression of Tex19.1 reduced the ability of both a codon-optimized Tf type and a natural Gf type mouse L1 to mobilize in these cells, suggesting that Tex19.1 restricts retrotransposition of multiple active L1 subtypes (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by L1 retrotransposition assay data in Figure 5B

claim: Tex19.1 restricts retrotransposition of multiple active L1 subtypes.
source: suggesting that Tex19.1 restricts retrotransposition of multiple active L1 subtypes (Figure 5B).
evidence: Inferred from retrotransposition assay data showing restriction of multiple L1 subtypes

claim: Mouse Tex19.1 restricts mobilization of engineered human L1 constructs.
source: Mouse Tex19.1 also restricts mobilization of engineered human L1 constructs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) although less efficiently than it restricts mouse L1s.
evidence: Supported by L1 retrotransposition assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: Tex19.1 can function as a restriction factor for L1 mobilization in cultured cells.
source: Altogether, these data show that Tex19.1 can function as a restriction factor for L1 mobilization in cultured cells.
evidence: Inferred from multiple retrotransposition assay results

claim: Mouse Tex19.1 restricts mobilization of mouse and human L1 constructs by ~50% in HeLa cells.
source: L1 retrotransposition assays using a blasticidin retrotransposition indicator cassette (Beck et al., 2010; Goodier et al., 2007; Morrish et al., 2002) in HeLa cells (Figure 5C) showed that mouse Tex19.1 similarly restricts mobilization of mouse and human L1 constructs by ~50% in this epithelial carcinoma cell line (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by L1 retrotransposition assay data in Figure 5D and citations to Beck et al., 2010; Goodier et al., 2007; Morrish et al., 2002

claim: Human TEX19 restricts mobilization of mouse and human L1 constructs by ~50% in HeLa cells.
source: Human TEX19 also restricts mobilization of mouse and human L1 constructs by ~ 50% in HeLa cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by L1 retrotransposition assay data in Figure 5D

claim: TEX19 orthologs are host restriction factors for L1 retrotransposition in mice and humans.
source: Thus, TEX19 orthologs are host restriction factors for L1 retrotransposition in mice and humans.
evidence: Inferred from retrotransposition assay data in multiple cell types

claim: Mouse UBR2 co-IPs with mL1-ORF1p in HEK293T cells.
source: Interestingly, mouse UBR2 co-IPs with mL1-ORF1p in HEK293T cells (Figure 6A), a cell type that does not express any detectable TEX19 protein (Reichmann et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data in Figure 6A and citation to Reichmann et al., 2017

claim: UBR2 is able to regulate L1-ORF1p independently of any effects on TEX19 protein stability.
source: Thus, these data strongly suggest that UBR2 is able to regulate L1-ORF1p independently of any effects on TEX19 protein stability.
evidence: Inferred from the co-IP of UBR2 with L1-ORF1p in cells lacking TEX19

claim: UBR2 interacts with mL1-ORF1RAp mutants that have reduced binding to RNA.
source: UBR2 also interacts with mL1-ORF1RAp mutants that have reduced binding to RNA (Figure 6B)
evidence: Supported by co-IP data in Figure 6B

claim: The physical interaction between UBR2 and L1-ORF1p is not mediated by L1 RNA.
source: suggesting that this physical interaction is not mediated by L1 RNA.
evidence: Inferred from the interaction with RNA-binding mutant of L1-ORF1p

claim: The interactions between UBR2 and L1-ORF1p are conserved in human L1-ORF1p.
source: Furthermore, these interactions are conserved in human L1-ORF1p (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and 1C

claim: Overexpression of UBR2 alone restricts mobilization of an engineered human L1.
source: In addition, overexpression of UBR2 alone restricts mobilization of an engineered human L1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by L1 retrotransposition assay data in Figure 6C

claim: UBR2 is able to physically interact with L1-ORF1p and restrict mobilization of L1 constructs in cultured cells.
source: Thus, at least in overexpression experiments, UBR2 is able to physically interact with L1-ORF1p and restrict mobilization of L1 constructs in cultured cells.
evidence: Inferred from co-IP and retrotransposition assay data

claim: mL1-ORF1p abundance is post-transcriptionally elevated approximately four fold in the cerebellum of Ubr2−/− mice.
source: Consistent with the physical interaction between UBR2 and mL1-ORF1p (Figure 6A), we found that mL1-ORF1p abundance is post-transcriptionally elevated approximately four fold in the cerebellum of Ubr2−/− mice (Figure 6D)
evidence: Supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data in Figure 6D

claim: UBR2 may directly regulate polyubiquitylation and subsequent degradation of mL1-ORF1p in vivo.
source: suggesting that UBR2 may directly regulate polyubiquitylation and subsequent degradation of mL1-ORF1p in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the physical interaction between UBR2 and mL1-ORF1p and the increased mL1-ORF1p levels in Ubr2−/− mice

claim: Endogenous Ubr2 plays a Tex19.1-independent role in regulating mL1-ORF1p abundance in vivo.
source: Nevertheless, regardless of this additional complexity in the cerebrum, the increased abundance of mL1-ORF1p in Ubr2−/− cerebellum demonstrates that endogenous Ubr2 plays a Tex19.1-independent role in regulating mL1-ORF1p abundance in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the increased mL1-ORF1p in Ubr2−/− cerebellum, a tissue that does not express Tex19.1

claim: Expression of Tex19.1 in the germline or in response to DNA hypomethylation stimulates a pre-existing activity of UBR2 to regulate mL1-ORF1p.
source: Ubr2 has numerous endogenous cellular substrates and host functions beyond regulating mL1-ORF1p (Ouyang et al., 2006; Reichmann et al., 2017; Sriram et al., 2011), but expression of Tex19.1 in the germline or in response to DNA hypomethylation appears to stimulate a pre-existing activity of UBR2 to regulate mL1-ORF1p, possibly at the expense of UBR2's activity towards some endogenous cellular substrates (Reichmann et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the data showing UBR2 can regulate L1-ORF1p independently of TEX19.1, with citations to Ouyang et al., 2006; Reichmann et al., 2017; Sriram et al., 2011

claim: Endogenous mL1-ORF1p is polyubiquitylated in pluripotent mouse ESCs.
source: Biochemical isolation of polyubiquitylated proteins suggests that endogenous mL1-ORF1p is polyubiquitylated in pluripotent mouse ESCs (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by TUBE2 pull-down data in Figure 7A

claim: Proteasome inhibition with lactacystin causes a ~4 fold increase in the abundance of mL1-ORF1p relative to β-actin after 6 hr of treatment in mouse ESCs.
source: Furthermore, proteasome inhibition with lactacystin caused a ~4 fold increase in the abundance of mL1-ORF1p relative to β-actin after 6 hr of treatment (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 7B

claim: mL1-ORF1p abundance is regulated by the proteasome in pluripotent mouse ESCs.
source: Taken together these data suggest that mL1-ORF1p abundance is regulated by the proteasome in pluripotent mouse ESCs.
evidence: Inferred from polyubiquitylation and proteasome inhibition data

claim: Tex19.1−/− mouse ESCs do not de-repress L1 RNA.
source: In contrast to a previous report assessing the abundance of retrotransposon RNA in ESCs derived from heterozygous mouse crosses (Tarabay et al., 2013), Tex19.1−/− mouse ESCs generated by sequential gene targeting (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) in a defined genetic background, cultured in 2i conditions, and analysed at low passage number do not de-repress L1 RNA (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 7C, contrasting with citation to Tarabay et al., 2013

claim: Tex19.1−/− mouse ESCs contain elevated levels of endogenous mL1-ORF1p without increased endogenous L1 mRNA levels.
source: These Tex19.1−/− mouse ESCs contain elevated levels of endogenous mL1-ORF1p, but this increase in mL1-ORF1p levels is not accompanied by increased endogenous L1 mRNA levels (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and qRT-PCR data in Figure 7C

claim: Loss of Tex19.1 does not detectably affect transcription or translation of L1 reporter constructs in ESCs.
source: Moreover, loss of Tex19.1 does not detectably affect transcription or translation of L1 reporter constructs in ESCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3

claim: Tex19.1 functions to post-translationally repress mL1-ORF1p in pluripotent cells.
source: Taken together these data suggest that, similar to male germ cells (Figure 1), Tex19.1 functions to post-translationally repress mL1-ORF1p in pluripotent cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mL1-ORF1p levels increase without changes in L1 RNA levels in Tex19.1−/− ESCs

claim: Mobilization of an active mouse Tf L1 is reproducibly elevated around 1.5-fold in Tex19.1−/− ESCs relative to Tex19.1+/+ wild-type ESCs.
source: Interestingly, mobilization of an active mouse Tf L1 is reproducibly elevated around 1.5-fold in Tex19.1−/− ESCs relative to Tex19.1+/+ wild-type ESCs (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by L1 retrotransposition assay data in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 4B

claim: Tex19.1 controls L1 retrotransposition in mouse pluripotent ESCs, presumably at least in part by promoting proteasome degradation of mL1-ORF1p.
source: Thus, these data strongly suggest that Tex19.1 controls L1 retrotransposition in mouse pluripotent ESCs, presumably at least in part by promoting proteasome degradation of mL1-ORF1p.
evidence: Inferred from the increased L1 retrotransposition in Tex19.1−/− ESCs and the role of Tex19.1 in regulating mL1-ORF1p levels

claim: Loss of Tex19.1 does not influence the rate of retrotransposition of the ORF1p-independent engineered zebrafish LINE-2 construct in mouse ESCs.
source: Remarkably, loss of Tex19.1 does not influence the rate of retrotransposition of the ORF1p-independent engineered zebrafish LINE-2 construct in mouse ESCs (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by L1 retrotransposition assay data in Figure 7D

claim: One role of endogenously expressed Tex19.1 in mouse pluripotent cells is to restrict L1 mobilization, and thereby promote genome stability in the cells that can transmit new L1 integrations to the next generation.
source: Thus, these data suggest that one role of endogenously expressed Tex19.1 in mouse pluripotent cells is to restrict L1 mobilization, and thereby promote genome stability in the cells that can transmit new L1 integrations to the next generation.
evidence: Inferred from the increased L1 retrotransposition in Tex19.1−/− ESCs and the lack of effect on ORF1p-independent retrotransposition

claim: Tex19.1 is a host restriction factor for L1 mobilization in the mammalian germline.
source: This study identifies Tex19.1 as a host restriction factor for L1 mobilization in the mammalian germline.
evidence: Inferred from multiple lines of evidence showing Tex19.1 restricts L1 mobilization in pluripotent cells and germ cells

claim: Tex19.1 plays a role in regulating the abundance of retrotransposon RNAs.
source: We have previously reported that Tex19.1 plays a role in regulating the abundance of retrotransposon RNAs (Ollinger et al., 2008; Reichmann et al., 2012, 2013), which appears to reflect transcriptional de-repression of specific retrotransposons (Crichton et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ollinger et al., 2008; Reichmann et al., 2012, 2013; Crichton et al., 2017a

claim: Loss of Tex19.1 results in de-repression of L1 RNA in placenta.
source: Although loss of Tex19.1 results in de-repression of L1 RNA in placenta (Reichmann et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Reichmann et al., 2013

claim: L1 RNA abundance is not affected by loss of Tex19.1 in male germ cells.
source: L1 RNA abundance is not affected by loss of Tex19.1 in male germ cells (Ollinger et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ollinger et al., 2008

claim: Tex19.1 appears to regulate retrotransposons at multiple stages of their life cycle.
source: Thus, Tex19.1 appears to regulate retrotransposons at multiple stages of their life cycle.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Tex19.1 affects both transcriptional and post-translational regulation of retrotransposons

claim: Loss of Tex19.1 results in a 1.5-fold increase in the rate of mobilization of L1 constructs in pluripotent cells.
source: However, loss of Tex19.1 results in a 1.5-fold increase in the rate of mobilization of L1 constructs in pluripotent cells.
evidence: Supported by L1 retrotransposition assay data in Figure 7D

claim: L1 mobilization mostly takes place in the pluripotent phase of the germline cycle.
source: Since L1 mobilization mostly takes place in the pluripotent phase of the germline cycle
evidence: Stated as established knowledge in the field

claim: TEX19 activity could be having a significant impact on L1-derived mutations during evolution.
source: and new L1-dependent mobilization events are thought to be inherited by one in every twenty human births (Kazazian, 1999), TEX19 activity could be having a significant impact on L1-derived mutations during evolution.
evidence: Speculated based on the frequency of L1 mobilization events and the role of TEX19 in restricting L1 mobilization, with citation to Kazazian, 1999

claim: L1-ORF1p is post-translationally modified by ubiquitylation in somatic and germline cells.
source: Our data suggests that L1-ORF1p is post-translationally modified by ubiquitylation in somatic and germline cells.
evidence: Inferred from ubiquitylation assay data in multiple cell types

claim: Phosphorylation of L1-ORF1p has been previously reported in somatic tissues and is required for L1 retrotransposition in these cells.
source: Phosphorylation of L1-ORF1p has been previously reported in somatic tissues and is required for L1 retrotransposition in these cells (Cook et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cook et al., 2015

claim: There are 32 lysine residues in human L1-ORF1p that could act as potential ubiquitylation sites.
source: There are 32 lysine residues in human L1-ORF1p that could act as potential ubiquitylation sites (deHaro et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citation to deHaro et al., 2014

claim: There are 42, 47 and 39 lysines in mouse Tf, Gf and A subtypes of L1-ORF1p respectively that could act as potential ubiquitylation sites.
source: and 42, 47 and 39 lysines in mouse Tf, Gf and A subtypes of L1-ORF1p respectively that could act as potential ubiquitylation sites.
evidence: Stated as factual information about L1-ORF1p sequence
